To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) the effects of radiative heat transfer on the flow field are significant, (b) the effects of TRI on the flow field and radiative heat transfer are significant, and (c) the effects of finite rate chemistry on the flow field, radiative heat flux, and the species concentrations are significant.

(i) the finite rate chemistry, (ii) radiative heat transfer (iii) turbulence-radiation interaction (TRI) models, and (iv) the wall transition model were successfully incorporated into a computational fluid dynamics (CFD) solver for hypersonic flow, and that (v) the predictions of density, velocity, and radiative source terms were in good agreement with measurements.

(1) the radiative source term in the turbulent boundary region was found to be significant, (2) the TRI model predicted a significant enhancement in emission due to temperature fluctuations in the boundary layer, and (3) the density predictions were sensitive to the modeling assumptions employed, but the variations diminished along the body.
In summary, our research is concerned with
developing a computationally efficient approach to modeling radiative transport, finite rate chemistry, and turbulence-radiation interactions (TRI).
the development of computational tools that can be used in the design of hypersonic vehicles.
the effects of radiative transfer, turbulence-radiation interactions, finite-rate chemistry, and transition onset modeling on the flowfield and wall heat transfer of the Mach 2 Reentry F flight.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the effects of finite rate chemistry and radiation on the flow field are small, while the effects of turbulence radiation interaction are significant, and that the modeling options for the latter are not fully converged.
the current computational tools are capable of predicting the flow physics of the Mach 2 Reentry F flight with a good degree of accuracy.
finite rate chemistry, TRI, and radiative effects must be considered in future simulations of the Reentry F flight.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the effects of finite rate chemistry and TRI on the density and velocity profiles are relatively small, while the radiative effects are significant and the effects of finite chemistry on the species concentrations are substantial in this case.
the finite-rate chemistry, TRI, and radiative transfer effects were important for this flight regime and should be accounted for in future simulations.
the finite rate chemistry, TRI, and radiative heat transfer models are capable of predicting the experimental results with good agreement.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the radiative source terms are significant and that TRI is important in the turbulent boundary layers of hypersonic vehicles.
the chemistry model choice can be critical for the accurate assessment of the flow field in the turbulent boundary layers of high-speed reentry vehicles.
the radiative source term is not the only quantity affected by finite-rate chemistry.
